header.system:
You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You are the integrating analyst of a code-safety review. Six departments have each committed `findings/<department>.json` and `report/<department>.md` on their own branch, and this worktree is the merge of all of them. You write two files and nothing else: `findings.json` and `SAFETY-REPORT.md`.

Read `REPORTING.md` in this worktree first: it states the finding format, the exact sections of the report, the count lines both summaries carry, and the certificate's wording. Read `target.json` for the tree under review and the SHA-256 the certificate states. Read every `findings/*.json` and every `report/*.md` before writing anything. When a `report-template` skill is available, load it: it owns how the report reads, while `REPORTING.md` owns what the examiner mechanically decides and wins wherever the two differ in form.

Ask the examiner which findings do not hold before you write the union:

    for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done

Every id it prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason. Dropping one silently fails the report.

`findings.json` is the union, deduplicated by `file` plus `line` plus `cwe`, keeping the entry whose `confidence` is higher. Copy each entry whole; do not rewrite a department's `snippet`, because the examiner compares it with the target's own text.

The report is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by the committed examiner, over the files the departments actually read. `## Scope and method` says that, names the departments that ran and the tools that ran, and states what was read rather than what exists. `## What was not covered` is not a formality: name the file kinds nobody opened, the classes of defect no department owns, the checks that did not run, and every dropped finding. Never write that the target is secure, safe or free of vulnerabilities — nothing this program did could support it, and the examiner refuses the claim.

Before you stop, run `node verify-safety-report.mjs --report`, fix every line it names, and commit everything. Work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured. Never write into the target tree, and never edit `verify-safety-report.mjs`, `target.json` or any department's committed files.


Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern. A pattern with no "/" matches basenames at any depth, so "*" matches every file in the tree rather than its top level. Results are files only, never directories, and include hidden and ignored files: a result that fits comes back in modification-time order, while a larger one is sampled across top-level entries, so it spans the tree instead of one subtree.

Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents. Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result instead returns 100 paths sampled across top-level entries, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns the first 250 matches inline; a capped result reports where the complete match list was saved. Use read on a matched file for surrounding context.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file.

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

content.description: Full UTF-8 text content to write.

1: # How this program reports what it found
2: 
3: This worktree is the **report repository**. The code under review is the **target tree**, which is somewhere else on this host: `target.json` beside this file states its absolute path, the files it covers, and the SHA-256 the whole tree locks to.
4: 
5: The target is read-only for every session of this program. `verify-safety-report.mjs` re-hashes every locked file on every run, so a target a department edited fails the program instead of releasing a report about a tree that no longer exists.
6: 
7: ## This file and the skills
8: 
9: When the deployment mounts the code-safety knowledge pack, its `review-method`, `severity-and-evidence` and `report-template` skills own the craft: how to read a codebase, how to score a severity, what evidence has to name, and how the report reads. Follow them.
10: 
11: This file owns what `verify-safety-report.mjs` mechanically decides, and it is binding wherever the two differ in form. There is one such place and it is stated below: the counts each summary carries are written as `- <severity>: <count>` lines so the examiner can compare them with the union, which is the machine-readable form of the skill's "counts per severity".
12: 
13: ## What a department delivers
14: 
15: Two files, both committed on the department's own branch:
16: 
17: - `findings/<department>.json` — a JSON array of findings, `[]` when the department found nothing.
18: - `report/<department>.md` — the department's own prose: what it looked at, what it found, and what it did not reach.
19: 
20: Nothing else. Do not write `SAFETY-REPORT.md`, `findings.json`, `target.json` or `verify-safety-report.mjs`: the first two are the integration's, and the last two are the examiner.
21: 
22: ## The evidence rule
23: 
24: A finding without a file and a line is not a finding. Quote the exact line you cite; `verify-safety-report.mjs` compares your `snippet` with the target's own text at that line, ignoring only whitespace, and refuses the whole file when they differ.
25: 
26: Prefer three findings you have read the code for over twelve a pattern matched. `confidence` is what you actually know: `confirmed` when you read the sink, the source and the path between them; `likely` when the sink is dangerous and the source is plausibly attacker-controlled; `possible` when the pattern is there and the reachability is not established.
27: 
28: ## The finding
29: 
30: ```json
31: {
32:   "id": "secrets-cookie-secret",
33:   "cwe": "CWE-798",
34:   "owasp": "A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures",
35:   "severity": "high",
36:   "confidence": "confirmed",
37:   "title": "Session cookie secret is hard-coded in the committed configuration",
38:   "file": "config/env/all.js",
39:   "line": 8,
40:   "snippet": "cookieSecret: \"session_cookie_secret_key_here\",",
41:   "evidence": "The value is a literal in a committed file and is the secret express-session is configured with.",
42:   "impact": "Anyone with the repository can forge a session cookie and authenticate as any user.",
43:   "fix": "Read the secret from the environment and rotate the committed value.",
44:   "references": ["https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/798.html"]
45: }
46: ```
47: 
48: | Field | Rule |
49: | --- | --- |
50: | `id` | letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores, unique across the whole program; prefix it with your department or use the pack's `SEC-<n>` numbering. |
51: | `cwe` | `CWE-<number>`. |
52: | `owasp` | the OWASP Top 10 category, named. |
53: | `severity` | `critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low` or `info`. |
54: | `confidence` | `confirmed`, `likely` or `possible`. |
55: | `title` | one line a reader can act on. |
56: | `file` | path relative to the target root, exactly as `target.json` lists it. |
57: | `line` | 1-based line in that file. |
58: | `endLine` | optional last line when the finding spans several; `snippet` then quotes all of them. |
59: | `snippet` | the target's own text at those lines, verbatim. |
60: | `evidence` | why this line is the vulnerability, naming what you read. |
61: | `impact` | what an attacker gets. |
62: | `fix` | what to change. |
63: | `references` | array of URLs or identifiers; may be empty. |
64: 
65: ## Checking your own work before you commit
66: 
67: ```sh
68: node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/<department>.json
69: ```
70: 
71: That is the same command your goal is measured by. Run it, fix what it names, then commit everything — work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured.
72: 
73: ## What the integration delivers
74: 
75: The integration merges every department branch and then writes two files of its own.
76: 
77: `findings.json` is the union of every `findings/<department>.json`, deduplicated by `file` + `line` + `cwe`, keeping the entry with the higher `confidence`. Before writing it, ask the examiner which findings do not hold:
78: 
79: ```sh
80: for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done
81: ```
82: 
83: Every id that command prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason the examiner gave. Dropping one silently fails the report: `--report` refuses a union that omits an id no section discloses.
84: 
85: `SAFETY-REPORT.md` carries exactly these sections, in this order:
86: 
87: ```markdown
88: ## Résumé exécutif
89: 
90: <deux paragraphes en français : ce qui a été examiné, ce qui a été trouvé, ce que cela implique>
91: 
92: - critical: 0
93: - high: 0
94: - medium: 0
95: - low: 0
96: - info: 0
97: 
98: ## Executive summary
99: 
100: <the same in English>
101: 
102: - critical: 0
103: - high: 0
104: - medium: 0
105: - low: 0
106: - info: 0
107: 
108: ## Scope and method
109: 
110: <the target, its locked file count, which departments ran, which tools ran — the scanner, the advisory source — and which files were actually read>
111: 
112: ## Findings
113: 
114: ### critical
115: 
116: - `<id>` — <title> (`<file>:<line>`, <cwe>, <confidence>) — <impact, then fix>
117: 
118: ### high
119: 
120: ...
121: 
122: ## What was not covered
123: 
124: - <a department, a file kind, a class of vulnerability, or a check that did not run, and why>
125: - <every dropped finding id, with the examiner's reason>
126: 
127: ## Certificate
128: 
129: Verified findings: <count>
130: Target tree: <the sha256 from target.json>
131: 
132: <one sentence on what was checked mechanically: that every finding resolves to a real file and line in the locked tree, that every id is unique, and that no two findings share file, line and CWE>
133: 
134: This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".
135: ```
136: 
137: Both summary sections state a `- <severity>: <count>` line for all five severities, and the five counts must be the counts `findings.json` actually holds. Every finding id in `findings.json` is cited in `## Findings`. Every `<file>:<line>` written anywhere in the report must resolve in the target, so write a path you did not read as prose rather than as a citation.
138: 
139: The report is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by this examiner. Say so in `## Scope and method`. Never write that the target is secure, safe, or free of vulnerabilities: `verify-safety-report.mjs` refuses those claims, because nothing this program did could support one.
140: 
141: Check it before you commit:
142: 
143: ```sh
144: node verify-safety-report.mjs --report
145: ```

(End of file - total 145 lines)

<skill_instructions>
# The report layout

Every report has exactly these sections, in this order. Do not add marketing language, severity totals presented as a score out of ten, or a remediation timeline the review has no authority to commit the customer to.

- **`## Résumé exécutif`** — French. Counts per severity, the three most important findings by name and effect, what was and was not covered in one sentence each, and one paragraph on method.
- **`## Executive summary`** — the same content in English, for a mixed-language or non-French reader.
- **`## Scope and method`** — the repository, commit or tag reviewed, which directories or services were in scope, and a link to [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).
- **`## Findings`** — grouped by severity, critical first; one bullet per finding with its id, title, `file:line`, CWE, and confidence. Full detail (snippet, evidence, impact, fix) lives in the accompanying JSON per [severity-and-evidence](../severity-and-evidence/SKILL.md), not duplicated in prose here.
- **`## What was not covered`** — the [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md) not-covered list, specific to this engagement.
- **`## Certificate`** — what a mechanical verifier checked after the fact: every finding resolves to a real file and line in the reviewed commit, every id is unique, every CWE/OWASP id is a known identifier, and no two findings share file, line, and CWE. This certifies the report's internal consistency, not the completeness or correctness of the review's judgment.

## Filled example: a small Express app

```markdown
## Résumé exécutif

Cette revue a porté sur le code source de commande-api, une application Express.js
de gestion de commandes, au commit a1b2c3d. Elle a permis d'identifier 3 constats :
1 critique, 1 moyen et 1 faible. Les plus importants : (1) une injection SQL
critique dans la recherche de commande par identifiant (src/routes/orders.js:42),
permettant de lire ou modifier toute donnée accessible par l'utilisateur de base de
données de l'application ; (2) une fixation de session lors de la connexion
(src/routes/auth.js:58) ; (3) l'absence de l'en-tête HSTS (src/app.js:12). La revue
a couvert les points d'entrée HTTP, l'authentification et la gestion des sessions ;
elle n'a pas couvert l'infrastructure de déploiement ni les dépendances tierces
(voir « Ce qui n'a pas été couvert »). Méthode : lecture des points d'entrée,
suivi des données de la source jusqu'au point d'exécution, un constat par point
d'exécution, ligne exactement citée et niveau de confiance déclaré pour chacun.

## Executive summary

This review covered commande-api, an Express.js order-management application, at
commit a1b2c3d, and found 3 issues: 1 critical, 1 medium, 1 low. The most
important: (1) a critical SQL injection in order lookup by id
(src/routes/orders.js:42); (2) session fixation on login
(src/routes/auth.js:58); (3) a missing HSTS header (src/app.js:12). HTTP entry
points, authentication, and session handling were covered; deployment
infrastructure and third-party dependencies were not (see "What was not covered").

## Scope and method

Repository commande-api, commit a1b2c3d, `src/` only. Method: [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).

## Findings

### Critical
- SEC-001 — SQL injection in order lookup — `src/routes/orders.js:42` — CWE-89 — confirmed

### Medium
- SEC-002 — Session id not rotated after login (session fixation) — `src/routes/auth.js:58` — CWE-384 — likely

### Low
- SEC-003 — Missing Strict-Transport-Security header — `src/app.js:12` — CWE-319 — confirmed

## What was not covered

- `infra/` (Terraform, Dockerfiles) and CI/CD configuration.
- Third-party dependency advisories (separate engagement).
- Runtime configuration: actual deployed environment variables, WAF rules, and network topology.
- Native mobile or memory-safety classes of bug: this codebase has no native module.

## Certificate

Mechanically verified: 3/3 findings resolve to an existing line at commit a1b2c3d;
3/3 ids unique; 3/3 CWE and OWASP ids recognized; 0 findings share file, line, and
CWE. This certifies internal consistency only, not completeness of coverage.

2: // Mechanical examiner of a code-safety report. It is in the report
3: // repository's base commit, so no department can change what measures it.
4: //
5: //   node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings <path>  one department's findings
6: //   node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings <path> --list-invalid
7: //   node verify-safety-report.mjs --report           the merged report
8: //
9: // `--findings` decides one findings file against the target tree. Adding
10: // `--list-invalid` turns the same decision into a report: the failing ids go to
11: // stdout, one per line, and the exit code is 0, which is how the integration
12: // learns which findings to drop and disclose.
13: //
14: // `--report` decides SAFETY-REPORT.md and findings.json together, including the
15: // disclosure rule: every id any `findings/<department>.json` carries and
16: // findings.json does not must be named under `## What was not covered`.
17: //
18: // Exit 0 only when every rule holds; otherwise every failure is printed to
19: // stderr, one per line, and the exit code is 1. Node built-ins only, because
20: // this runs in a worktree that installs nothing.
21: import { createHash } from 'node:crypto'
22: import { existsSync, readdirSync, readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
23: import { basename, join, relative, resolve } from 'node:path'

25: /** Severities a finding may claim, most severe first. */
26: const SEVERITIES = ['critical', 'high', 'medium', 'low', 'info']
27: 
28: /** How sure a finding's author is that the cited code is exploitable as described. */
29: const CONFIDENCES = ['confirmed', 'likely', 'possible']
30: 
31: /** Sections SAFETY-REPORT.md carries, in this order. */
32: const SECTIONS = [
33:   '## Résumé exécutif',
34:   '## Executive summary',
35:   '## Scope and method',
36:   '## Findings',
37:   '## What was not covered',
38:   '## Certificate',
39: ]

41: /** The claim the certificate must make verbatim, and the only claim this review supports. */
42: const HONESTY = 'This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".'
43: 
44: /** Claims no coverage this review can state would support. */
45: const OVERCLAIMS = /\bno vulnerabilities\b|\bfree of vulnerabilities\b|\b(?:is|are|was|were) secure\b|\bsafe to deploy\b|\bproven secure\b|\bfully audited\b/i
46: 
47: /** Text a report still carrying its template is refused for. */
48: const PLACEHOLDER = /\bTODO\b|\bTBD\b|\bFIXME\b|lorem ipsum|<placeholder>|PLACEHOLDER/i
49: 
50: /** String fields every finding states in prose. */
51: const PROSE_FIELDS = ['title', 'evidence', 'impact', 'fix']
52: 
53: /** How a file's text is compared with a finding's quoted snippet. */
54: const normalize = (text) => text.replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim()
55: 
56: /** Lowercase hex SHA-256 of one buffer or string. */
57: const sha256 = (content) => createHash('sha256').update(content).digest('hex')
58: 
59: /**
60:  * Every file under one directory, relative and sorted, skipping the excluded names.
61:  * @param {string} root directory to walk
62:  * @param {string[]} exclude directory basenames never descended into
63:  * @returns {string[]} relative POSIX-ish paths, sorted
64:  */
65: function walk(root, exclude) {
66:   const found = []
67:   const descend = (directory) => {
68:     for (const entry of readdirSync(directory, { withFileTypes: true }).sort((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name))) {
69:       const path = join(directory, entry.name)
70:       if (entry.isDirectory()) {
71:         if (!exclude.includes(entry.name)) descend(path)
72:       } else if (entry.isFile()) found.push(relative(root, path))
73:     }
74:   }
75:   descend(root)
76:   return found.sort()
77: }

79: /** One target tree as the lock and the verifier both read it: the files, their digests, and their text. */
80: class Target {
81:   /**
82:    * @param {string} reportRoot the report repository the lock is committed in
83:    * @param {string[]} failures collector every rule appends to
84:    */
85:   constructor(reportRoot, failures) {
86:     this.failures = failures
87:     this.root = undefined
88:     this.files = new Map()
89:     this.lines = new Map()
90:     const lockPath = join(reportRoot, 'target.json')
91:     if (!existsSync(lockPath)) {
92:       failures.push('target.json is missing from this worktree; the base commit carries the lock of the tree under review')

95:     const lock = JSON.parse(readFileSync(lockPath, 'utf8'))
96:     this.root = lock.root
97:     this.exclude = lock.exclude ?? []

105:    * cites a line of the tree this program was asked to review, and a tree a

108:   checkTree() {
109:     if (!existsSync(this.root)) {
110:       this.failures.push(`the target tree ${this.root} is not on this host, so no citation can be resolved`)
111:       this.root = undefined
112:       return
113:     }
114:     const present = walk(this.root, this.exclude)
115:     for (const path of present) {
116:       if (!this.files.has(path)) this.failures.push(`the target tree gained ${path} since the base commit locked it`)
117:     }
118:     for (const [path, hash] of this.files) {
119:       if (!present.includes(path)) {
120:         this.failures.push(`the target tree lost ${path} since the base commit locked it`)
121:         continue
122:       }
123:       if (sha256(readFileSync(join(this.root, path))) !== hash) {
124:         this.failures.push(`the target tree's ${path} changed since the base commit locked it; the target is read-only for this program`)
125:       }
126:     }
127:   }

131:    * @param {string} path path relative to the target root
132:    * @returns {string[] | undefined} the file's lines, or undefined when it is not in the locked tree
133:    */
134:   linesOf(path) {
135:     if (this.root === undefined || !this.files.has(path)) return undefined
136:     if (!this.lines.has(path)) this.lines.set(path, readFileSync(join(this.root, path), 'utf8').split('\n'))
137:     return this.lines.get(path)

142:    * @param {string} path path relative to the target root
143:    * @param {number} line 1-based line number
144:    * @returns {boolean} whether the file is under review and holds that line
145:    */
146:   resolves(path, line) {

148:     return lines !== undefined && Number.isInteger(line) && line >= 1 && line <= lines.length
149:   }

152: /**
153:  * Decide one finding against the target tree.
154:  * @param {unknown} finding one entry of a findings file
155:  * @param {number} index its position, named when the entry has no usable id
156:  * @param {Target} target the locked tree the finding cites

158:  * @returns {string[]} every rule this finding broke, empty when it holds

160: function checkFinding(finding, index, target, seen) {
161:   const failures = []
162:   if (finding === null || typeof finding !== 'object' || Array.isArray(finding)) {
163:     return [`finding #${index + 1} is not a JSON object`]
164:   }

166:   const name = typeof id === 'string' && id !== '' ? id : `#${index + 1}`
167:   const fail = (rule) => void failures.push(`${name}: ${rule}`)
168:   // Letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`: wide enough for both the `SEC-001`

176:   if (!CONFIDENCES.includes(finding.confidence)) fail(`confidence must be one of ${CONFIDENCES.join(', ')}`)

// learns which findings to drop and disclose.
// `--report` decides SAFETY-REPORT.md and findings.json together, including the
// disclosure rule: every id any `findings/<department>.json` carries and
// findings.json does not must be named under `## What was not covered`.

// this runs in a worktree that installs nothing.

/** Claims no coverage this review can state would support. */

const uncovered = section(text, '## What was not covered')

lines.text: "title": "express-session secret is hard-coded in the committed configuration",

"evidence": "config/env/all.js exports cookieSecret as a literal string. config/config.js line 10 merges this file into the exported config with no override in config/env/production.js (which is an empty module.exports = {}). server.js line 17 destructures cookieSecret from that config and passes it straight into express-session at server.js line 82 (`secret: cookieSecret`). Because the value never leaves the committed source tree, anyone who has read the repository (public on GitHub for this project) has the exact secret express-session signs cookies with.",

"impact": "Anyone with the source code can compute a valid signature for any req.session payload, forge a session cookie with an arbitrary userId (including an admin's), and be treated by the app as that authenticated user without ever knowing a password.",
"fix": "Read cookieSecret from an environment variable with no hard-coded fallback, generate it with a CSPRNG at deploy time, and rotate the value that was committed.",
"title": "The whole application, including login credentials and PII, is served over plain HTTP",

"evidence": "server.js starts the app exclusively with Node's plain http module; the https.createServer block that would load artifacts/cert/server.key and artifacts/cert/server.crt is commented out at lines 18-28 and 149-155. Every route mounted on this server travels in cleartext: app/routes/session.js posts userName/password to /login, and app/routes/profile.js lines 100-103 render the user's ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting fields (read from the database in app/data/profile-dao.js) back into the HTTP response body. The express-session cookie set at server.js line 78-102 also has no `secure` flag and travels on this same unencrypted channel.",

"impact": "Any network-level attacker (shared Wi-Fi, a compromised router, an ISP, or a MITM position) can read login credentials, session cookies, and SSNs/bank account and routing numbers in transit, and can replay a captured session cookie to take over the account.",

"fix": "Terminate TLS in front of the app (or re-enable the commented-out https.createServer block with a real certificate), redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS, and set the session cookie's `secure` flag.",
"title": "User passwords are stored in the database in plaintext",

"evidence": "addUser() builds the MongoDB user document with the raw `password` parameter taken directly from the signup request body (app/routes/session.js line 196-198, `const { ..., password, ... } = req.body`), with no hashing step; the bcrypt.hashSync(...) alternative is present only inside a comment at lines 27-30. This is confirmed by validateLogin() at line 61, `return fromDB === fromUser;`, which compares the value read back from usersCol against the login-form password with a plain string equality check -- the only comparison that works against a value stored this way.",

"impact": "Anyone who can read the users collection (a DB compromise, an unsecured backup, a NoSQL-injection read, or an insider with DB access) recovers every user's real password in cleartext, which is then usable to log into this app and, given password reuse, into other services under the same credentials.",

"fix": "Hash passwords with bcrypt (bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync())) or argon2id before insert, and compare with the library's constant-time compare function on login; never store or compare the raw password.",
"title": "SSN, date of birth and bank account/routing numbers are written to the database unencrypted",

"evidence": "updateUser() takes ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting straight from the /profile POST body (app/routes/profile.js lines 42-50) and assigns them verbatim to the document later written with `users.update({_id:...}, {$set: user}, ...)` at lines 78-91. The encrypt()/decrypt() helpers built around crypto.createCipheriv(config.cryptoAlgo, config.cryptoKey, ...) that would protect these fields exist only inside the comment block at lines 15-40 and are never called; getByUserId() at lines 94-110 likewise returns ssn/dob to the caller with the decrypt() call commented out at lines 100-105.",

"impact": "Anyone who can read the users collection (DB compromise, unsecured backup/export, or a NoSQL-injection read elsewhere in the app) obtains every user's Social Security number, date of birth and bank account/routing number in cleartext, enabling identity theft and financial fraud.",

"fix": "Encrypt ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting with an authenticated cipher (e.g. AES-256-GCM) using a key from a KMS/secrets manager and a fresh random nonce per record before the $set, decrypting only when displaying to the owning user.",
"title": "The merged application config, including the session-cookie secret, is printed to stdout on every start",

"evidence": "config is built at line 10 as `{ ...allConf, ...envConf }`, where allConf is config/env/all.js which defines `cookieSecret: \"session_cookie_secret_key_here\"` (line 8) and `cryptoKey: \"a_secure_key_for_crypto_here\"` (line 9); envConf for the development/test environments additionally contributes `zapApiKey` (config/env/development.js line 6, config/env/test.js line 6). util.inspect(config, false, null) at line 13 serializes the whole object, including these secrets, with no redaction, and console.log writes it to stdout on every application start.",

"impact": "Anyone with access to the process's stdout -- a hosting platform's log viewer (this app ships a Procfile for Heroku-style platforms), a container log driver, or a log-aggregation pipeline -- can read the session-signing secret and other keys straight out of the startup log.",
"fix": "Remove this log line in favor of an explicit allowlist of non-secret fields to log (e.g. port, environment name), or redact known-sensitive keys before logging.",
"title": "Unhandled errors are rendered verbatim to the client",

"evidence": "errorHandler is mounted as Express's error middleware at app/routes/index.js line 82 and receives every `err` passed to `next(err)` across the route handlers (e.g. DB errors from app/data/*.js callbacks, or a thrown value from the eval() calls in app/routes/contributions.js lines 32-34). It passes that raw Error object as `error` straight into app/views/error-template.html line 11, `
{{error}}`, and swig.setDefaults at server.js line 137 sets `autoescape: false`, so whatever the error's string representation contains is written unescaped into the HTML response.",

"impact": "A user who triggers a backend error (a malformed request, an unexpected DB failure, or a crafted value that breaks contributions.js's eval()) receives the internal error text in the response body, which can reveal implementation details -- library names, internal object structure, or fragments of the failing query -- that help an attacker refine further attacks.",

"fix": "Log the full error server-side only (console.error(err) is already done at lines 7-8) and render a fixed, generic message to the client; never pass the Error object itself into the response template.",
"title": "A default admin password is hard-coded in the database seed script that is documented to run in production",

"evidence": "The file's own header comment (lines 5-7) documents running it as `NODE_ENV=production node artifacts/db-reset.js`. "impact": "Anyone who has read this public repository knows a working admin username/password for any deployment that was seeded with this script and not had its admin password changed, giving immediate administrative access.",
"fix": "Never seed a production database with fixed, publicly-known credentials; generate a random admin password at provisioning time and require a forced change on first login.",
"title": "A static encryption key for PII encryption is hard-coded in committed configuration",

"evidence": "This key is only consumed by the encrypt()/decrypt() helpers inside the commented-out block of app/data/profile-dao.js (lines 15-40, `crypto.createCipheriv(config.cryptoAlgo, config.cryptoKey, config.iv)`), so it is not exercised by the code path as currently shipped (see data-004, where that block is disabled and ssn/dob are stored unencrypted instead). It is flagged as `possible` because enabling that commented-out fix as-is, without also externalizing this key, would encrypt every user's PII with a key that is public in this repository.",

"impact": "If the disabled encryption code in profile-dao.js were turned back on without changing this key, the SSN/DOB encryption it adds would be defeated by anyone who has read the source, since the same hard-coded key would be used for every record.",
"fix": "Load the encryption key from a secrets manager/KMS at runtime rather than from a committed config file, independent of whether the encryption code path is enabled.",

lines.text: "title": "NoSQL injection via unsanitized threshold in MongoDB $where clause",

"evidence": "app/routes/allocations.js reads `threshold` straight from `req.query` (const { threshold } = req.query;) at its line 20 and passes it unmodified as the second argument to allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold. That function (app/data/allocations-dao.js:57-84) interpolates the raw `threshold` string directly into a MongoDB `$where` JavaScript expression at line 78 with no validation, quoting escape or type coercion (the commented-out block above it, lines 63-76, is the disabled fix that used to call parseInt and range-check the value). The resulting object is passed straight to `allocationsCol.find(searchCriteria())` at line 86, so MongoDB evaluates the attacker's string as server-side JavaScript inside `$where`.",

"impact": "An attacker can submit GET /allocations/<userId>?threshold=' ; while(true){} // or an operator such as 0' ; return true; var x='0 to run arbitrary JavaScript inside the MongoDB server, causing denial of service or bypassing the intended filter to read every user's allocation data.",

"fix": "Never build a $where clause from request input. Validate `threshold` as a bounded integer (parseInt with a 0-99 range check, as the commented-out original fix does) and use a plain query object such as { userId: parsedUserId, stocks: { $gt: parsedThreshold } } instead of a $where string.",
"title": "Server-side JavaScript injection via eval() on contribution percentage (preTax)",

"evidence": "handleContributionsUpdate (app/routes/contributions.js:28) is mounted at POST /contributions with only the isLoggedIn guard (app/routes/index.js:52); no other middleware inspects the body. `req.body.preTax` is passed directly into Node's `eval()` at line 32 with no parsing, type-check or sanitization before or after the call; the only validation (isNaN/negative checks at line 47) runs after eval has already executed.",

"impact": "Any authenticated user can submit a POST /contributions request with preTax set to arbitrary JavaScript (e.g. `require('child_process').execSync('id')` or a process-crashing payload) and have it executed in the Node process, giving full server-side code execution under the application's privileges.",
"fix": "Never eval request data. Parse the value with Number()/parseInt() and reject non-numeric input, as the commented-out fix in the same file (lines 37-40) already shows.",
"title": "Server-side JavaScript injection via eval() on contribution percentage (afterTax)",

"evidence": "Same handler and route as the preTax finding: `req.body.afterTax` from the POST /contributions body reaches `eval()` unsanitized at line 33, with validation only applied afterwards at line 47.",
"impact": "Any authenticated user can execute arbitrary JavaScript on the server by setting afterTax to a malicious expression, achieving remote code execution.",
"fix": "Replace eval(req.body.afterTax) with Number(req.body.afterTax) or parseInt(req.body.afterTax, 10) plus a NaN check before use.",
"title": "Server-side JavaScript injection via eval() on contribution percentage (roth)",

"evidence": "Same handler and route as the preTax/afterTax findings: `req.body.roth` from the POST /contributions body reaches `eval()` unsanitized at line 34, with validation only applied afterwards at line 47.",
"impact": "Any authenticated user can execute arbitrary JavaScript on the server by setting roth to a malicious expression, achieving remote code execution.",
"fix": "Replace eval(req.body.roth) with Number(req.body.roth) or parseInt(req.body.roth, 10) plus a NaN check before use.",
"title": "Open redirect via unvalidated url query parameter",

"impact": "An attacker can craft a link such as /learn?url=https://evil.example/phish that, once clicked by a logged-in victim, redirects them from a trusted NodeGoat URL to an attacker-controlled site for phishing or credential harvesting.",
"fix": "Validate the target against an allowlist of known learning-resource hosts/paths, or only allow relative paths within the application, before calling res.redirect().",

lines.text: "title": "Helmet security-header middleware is entirely commented out; no CSP, frameguard, no-cache or X-Powered-By hardening is applied",

"evidence": "server.js:10 has `// const helmet = require(\"helmet\");` commented out, and the entire block that would call app.disable(\"x-powered-by\"), helmet.frameguard(), helmet.noCache(), helmet.contentSecurityPolicy() and helmet.hsts() (lines 38-65) is wrapped in a `/* ... */` block comment, so none of it executes. Line 14's `const nosniff = require('dont-sniff-mimetype')` is likewise commented out and app.use(nosniff()) at line 64 never runs. The only middleware actually mounted between express() at line 15 and the route handlers is favicon, body-parser and session (lines 68-102); no header-setting middleware of any kind is registered anywhere else in server.js or in app/routes. helmet (^2.0.0) and dont-sniff-mimetype are listed as dependencies in package.json but are never required in working code, confirming they are installed but unused.",

"impact": "Every response leaves X-Powered-By: Express (fingerprinting the framework/version), has no X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors (clickjacking via iframe embedding of authenticated pages such as /profile or /benefits), no Content-Security-Policy (no defense-in-depth against any XSS that does land, e.g. the reflected XSS this review found via profile firstName), and no X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff (browsers may MIME-sniff a response into an executable content type).",

"fix": "Uncomment and mount `helmet()` (or the modern helmet v4+ API: helmet.frameguard(), helmet.contentSecurityPolicy(), helmet.noSniff(), app.disable('x-powered-by')) before the route handlers in server.js, and pin a CSP that does not rely on 'unsafe-inline'.",
"title": "Server listens on plain HTTP only; HSTS and TLS are both disabled",

"evidence": "server.js explicitly labels this call \"Insecure HTTP connection\" in its own comment at line 144, and creates the listener with Node's plain `http` module (required at line 12) rather than `https`. The `https` alternative that would load a certificate/key from ./artifacts/cert (lines 18-28) and call https.createServer(httpsOptions, app).listen(...) (lines 149-155) is commented out. Combined with helmet.hsts() also being commented out (finding platform-001), the application has no path to Strict-Transport-Security and no TLS termination in the app itself, so session and auth cookies (server.js:78-90) travel in cleartext whenever the app is reached directly rather than behind a TLS-terminating proxy the code does not configure.",

"impact": "Session cookies, login credentials and profile PII (SSN, bank account/routing numbers handled by app/routes/profile.js) can be intercepted or modified in transit by a network attacker (MITM); a user who is ever tricked onto the http:// origin has no HSTS to force a later upgrade to HTTPS.",

"fix": "Terminate TLS (either in the app via https.createServer with a valid certificate, or at a reverse proxy) and add `app.use(helmet.hsts({ maxAge: 15552000, includeSubDomains: true }))` once TLS is in place.",
"title": "Session cookie is issued with the default name, no httpOnly, no secure and no sameSite attribute",

"evidence": "The express-session() options object passed here has no `cookie` key at all (the block at lines 92-100 that would add `cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true }` is commented out), so express-session falls back to its documented default cookie of `{ path: '/', httpOnly: true, secure: false }` with no `sameSite` set - meaning `secure` is explicitly false-by-default and no SameSite policy is applied. The `key` option that would rename the cookie away from the framework default `connect.sid` (lines 86-90) is also commented out, leaving the default session cookie name, which discloses the framework to a fingerprinting attacker. saveUninitialized: true additionally creates a session (and cookie) for every visitor before they log in.",

"impact": "Without `secure`, the session cookie is sent over plain HTTP (confirmed absent, see platform-002) and can be captured on the network. Without `sameSite`, the cookie is attached to cross-site requests, widening CSRF exposure (also see platform-004). The default `connect.sid` name confirms the backend framework to an attacker probing for known express-session vulnerabilities.",

"fix": "Set `cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'strict' }` and `key: \"sessionId\"` (or another non-default name) in the session() options, and only set `secure: true` once the app is served over HTTPS.",
"title": "CSRF protection middleware is commented out even though views still submit a _csrf token field",

"evidence": "`const csrf = require('csurf');` at line 7 is commented out and the app.use(csrf()) block that would validate a `_csrf` token on state-changing requests is also commented out (lines 104-113). `csurf` (^1.8.3) is a declared dependency in package.json but is never required in working code. app/views/profile.html:73 still renders `<input type=\"hidden\" name=\"_csrf\" value=\"{{csrftoken}}\" />`, but since `res.locals.csrftoken` is never populated (the middleware that sets it is disabled), this renders as an empty value and nothing on the server ever checks it, so POST /profile, POST /memos, POST /benefits and POST /contributions (app/routes/index.js) accept requests with no CSRF token verification at all.",

"impact": "A third-party site can force a logged-in victim's browser to submit POST /profile, /memos, /contributions or /benefits (all only gated by isLoggedIn, not by any CSRF check), letting an attacker change the victim's bank account/routing number, SSN, address or benefits allocation without the victim's consent.",
"fix": "Uncomment and mount `csurf()` before the routes that accept POST bodies, and keep populating `res.locals.csrftoken` for the templates that already expect it.",
"title": "Login does not regenerate the session id, enabling session fixation",

"evidence": "handleLoginRequest (app/routes/session.js:53-119) verifies credentials via userDAO.validateLogin and then writes `req.session.userId = user._id` onto the pre-existing session at line 116, with no call to `req.session.regenerate()` first. The surrounding comment block (lines 104-115) explicitly documents the fix (`req.session.regenerate(() => {})`) but it is not applied here - contrast with handleSignup in the same file, which does call `req.session.regenerate(() => { req.session.userId = user._id; ... })` at line 234. Since express-session's cookie has no `secure`/`sameSite` protection either (platform-003) and the app is served over plain HTTP (platform-002), an attacker-supplied session id set before authentication is carried straight through login unchanged.",

"impact": "An attacker who fixes a victim's session id before they authenticate (e.g. by getting the victim to visit the site once over the unprotected HTTP session cookie) gains a fully authenticated session as that victim after they log in, without ever learning their password.",
"fix": "Call `req.session.regenerate()` immediately after `userDAO.validateLogin` succeeds, before setting `req.session.userId`, the same way handleSignup already does at session.js:234.",
"title": "Global error handler renders the raw Error object to the browser",

"evidence": "The Express error-handling middleware (app/routes/error.js:3-13, mounted last in app/routes/index.js:82 as `app.use(ErrorHandler)`) logs `err.message` and `err.stack` to the server console (lines 7-8) but then also passes the entire `err` object into the `error-template` view as `error: err`. app/views/error-template.html:11 renders it directly as `
{{error}}` with swig's global autoescape disabled (server.js:135-142, see platform-007), and with no generic message or correlation id - any error surfaced by a route handler's `next(err)` (e.g. a MongoDB error bubbled up from a DAO) is shown to the requesting client verbatim instead of a generic message.",

"impact": "A triggered server error (a malformed id causing a MongoDB driver exception, for example) discloses internal error text - and, since the value is not the sanitized message, potentially internal object structure - directly to the end user, aiding further attack reconnaissance.",
"fix": "Log the full error server-side only, and render a generic message plus a correlation id to the client, e.g. `res.render(\"error-template\", { error: \"An unexpected error occurred\" })`.",
"title": "Template engine's autoescaping is globally disabled, and a profile field named \"SafeString\" is rendered unescaped",

"evidence": "swig.setDefaults({ autoescape: false }) applies to every `.html` view rendered by consolidate.swig (registered at server.js:116-117). This is reachable end to end: app/routes/profile.js:40-76 (handleProfileUpdate) destructures `firstName` straight from `req.body` (line 43) and, on the bank-routing validation-failure path, assigns `const firstNameSafeString = firstName;` at line 64 with no encoding despite the variable's name, then passes it to `res.render(\"profile\", { ..., firstNameSafeString, ... })` (lines 65-75). app/views/profile.html:41 renders it as `value=\"{{firstNameSafeString}}\"` and line 78 renders it a second time inside an `href` attribute (`<a href=\"{{firstNameSafeString}}\">`). Because autoescape is off, swig writes the attacker-supplied `firstName` into both HTML attributes without HTML-entity encoding.",

"impact": "An authenticated user can submit a `firstName` value such as `\"><script>...</script>` together with a bankRouting value that fails the routing-number regex, causing the server to re-render the profile form with the payload reflected unescaped into the page (both the input's `value` attribute and the `href` attribute), executing attacker JavaScript in that user's own session context and, via the same code path, in any admin or support user who views a shared/exported profile page rendered with the same template.",

"fix": "Re-enable `autoescape: true` in swig.setDefaults (the value the code's own comment marks as the fix), and additionally HTML-encode `firstName` (and the other profile fields rendered at profile.html:45-70) server-side before use in a URL context specifically, rather than relying on a single blanket HTML-encoding call.",
"title": "Configuration defaults to the development environment whenever NODE_ENV is unset or empty",

"evidence": "`finalEnv` falls back to the literal string \"development\" whenever `process.env.NODE_ENV` is falsy (unset or an empty string), and that value selects config/env/development.js to be merged over config/env/all.js at config.js:8-10. docker-compose.yml:7 declares the `NODE_ENV:` environment key with no value, which Compose passes through as an empty string unless the host shell happens to export it, so the containerized deployment silently lands in the development branch of `finalEnv` by default. config/env/development.js:9-13 then sets `environmentalScripts` to inject a livereload `<script>` tag containing `document.write(...)` built from `location.host`, and also carries a hard-coded ZAP proxy API key (development.js:6) into the running config that is logged in full by config.js:12-13 (`console.log(util.inspect(config, false, null))`).",

"impact": "Any deployment that forgets to explicitly export NODE_ENV=production (which the docker-compose.yml in this repository does not guarantee) runs with development-only settings active: a livereload script is injected into every rendered page, and the full merged configuration object - including secrets such as cookieSecret and cryptoKey from config/env/all.js - is written to the server's stdout/log on every boot.",

"fix": "Fail closed instead of defaulting to \"development\" (e.g. require NODE_ENV to be explicitly set, or default to \"production\"), and stop logging the full resolved config object, since it contains secrets.",
"title": "The /learn route redirects to a client-supplied URL with no validation",

"evidence": "The route handler passes `req.query.url` directly into `res.redirect()` with no allowlist, same-origin check, or format validation; the inline comment itself calls this \"Insecure way to handle redirects by taking redirect url from query string\". The only gate on the route is `isLoggedIn` (authentication), which does not restrict the redirect target.",

"impact": "An attacker can craft a link such as `https://nodegoat-host/learn?url=https://attacker.example/phish` that, when clicked by an authenticated user of the trusted domain, redirects them to an attacker-controlled site, useful for phishing or for bypassing URL allowlists that trust the NodeGoat origin.",
"fix": "Validate `req.query.url` against a fixed allowlist of destinations (or require it to be a known relative path) before calling res.redirect().",
"title": "No rate limiting or account lockout on the login route",

"evidence": "`POST /login` is wired straight to `sessionHandler.handleLoginRequest` (app/routes/session.js:53-119) with no middleware in between. No rate-limiting package (`express-rate-limit`, `express-brute`) appears anywhere in package.json, and no such middleware is `require`d or `app.use`d anywhere under server.js or app/routes (verified by grep across the whole repository); handleLoginRequest itself contains no failed-attempt counter, delay, or lockout logic - it simply calls userDAO.validateLogin and re-renders the login form on failure.",

"impact": "An attacker can send unlimited POST /login attempts to brute-force user passwords (or username enumeration, since the app distinguishes \"Invalid username\" from \"Invalid password\" at session.js:82-98) with no throttling, delay, CAPTCHA, or account lockout to slow them down.",

"fix": "Mount a rate limiter (e.g. express-rate-limit keyed by IP and by submitted username) on POST /login and POST /signup, and add a temporary lockout or increasing delay after repeated failed attempts for the same account.",

1: # Access department report — authentication, session handling and authorization
2: 
3: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (111 files locked in `target.json`, sha256 `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`), read-only for this review.
4: 
5: ## Method
6: 
7: `semgrep --version` reported `1.177.0`, so semgrep was run:
8: 
9: ```
10: semgrep --config <local rules>/code-safety.yml --config p/owasp-top-ten --metrics off --json /root/targets/NodeGoat
11: ```
12: 
13: 113 rules ran over 72 tracked files and produced 29 hits. Every hit was read as a lead, not accepted as a finding. The one directly relevant to this department was the `express-cookie-settings` family on `server.js:78` (no secure/httpOnly/expires/domain/path set on the session cookie), which is folded into the session-expiration finding below after reading `server.js` in full. The rest (GitHub Actions mutable tags, a NoSQL `$where` DAO, an `eval()` on request input, an open redirect, plaintext HTTP links in tutorial pages, a hard-coded cookie secret) belong to other departments (injection, secrets, platform) and were left to them.
14: 
15: After the scan, the review followed the route-by-route discipline: every `app.get`/`app.post`/`router.get` call in `app/routes/index.js` and `app/routes/tutorial.js` was enumerated with its exact middleware chain, then each handler file (`session.js`, `profile.js`, `benefits.js`, `allocations.js`, `contributions.js`, `memos.js`, `research.js`) and the DAO each one calls (`user-dao.js`, `profile-dao.js`, `benefits-dao.js`, `allocations-dao.js`) were read in full, plus `server.js` for session/cookie/CSRF wiring and `package.json`/`package-lock.json` for rate-limiting and CSRF dependencies actually in use.
16: 
17: ## Route table
18: 
19: | Method & path | Registration | Middleware chain (as read) | Unauthenticated caller | Wrong-identity authenticated caller |
20: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
21: | GET `/` | index.js:30 | none | sees the public welcome/login redirect | same, public by design |
22: | GET `/login` | index.js:33 | none | sees the form | n/a |
23: | POST `/login` | index.js:34 | none | can attempt to log in; **unlimited attempts, no lockout** | n/a |
24: | GET `/signup` | index.js:37 | none | sees the form | n/a |
25: | POST `/signup` | index.js:38 | none | can create an account | n/a |
26: | GET `/logout` | index.js:41 | none | destroys whatever session exists (harmless) | same |
27: | GET `/dashboard` | index.js:44 | isLoggedIn | redirected to `/login` | sees own dashboard only (session-derived id) |
28: | GET `/profile` | index.js:47 | isLoggedIn | redirected to `/login` | sees own profile only (session-derived id) |
29: | POST `/profile` | index.js:48 | isLoggedIn | redirected to `/login` | **can be forged cross-site: no CSRF token, session cookie has no SameSite** |
30: | GET `/contributions` | index.js:51 | isLoggedIn | redirected | own data only (session-derived id) |
31: | POST `/contributions` | index.js:52 | isLoggedIn | redirected | own data only, no CSRF token either (not filed separately; same missing global control as `/profile`) |
32: | GET `/benefits` | index.js:55 | isLoggedIn **only — isAdmin is commented out** | redirected | **any employee, not just admin, sees every non-admin employee's id/name/benefit date** |
33: | POST `/benefits` | index.js:56 | isLoggedIn **only — isAdmin is commented out** | redirected | **any employee can overwrite any other employee's `benefitStartDate` by supplying its `userId`** |
34: | GET `/allocations/:userId` | index.js:63 | isLoggedIn | redirected | **any employee can read any other employee's allocation by changing `:userId` in the URL (IDOR)** |
35: | GET `/memos`, POST `/memos` | index.js:66-67 | isLoggedIn | redirected | shared memo board by design (all employees see all memos); no per-user boundary is claimed by the app here, so not filed |
36: | GET `/learn` | index.js:70 | isLoggedIn | redirected | open redirect via `req.query.url` — filed to the injection/platform department (CWE-601), not repeated here |
37: | GET `/research` | index.js:76 | isLoggedIn | redirected | SSRF via `req.query.url` — filed to the injection department, not repeated here |
38: | `/tutorial/*` | index.js:79 | none | static documentation pages, no data access | same |
39: 
40: ## Findings
41: 
42: Eight findings, all `confirmed` — the source, every intermediate function and the sink were read for each. Full detail, evidence and fix are in `findings/access.json`; summary below.
43: 
44: 1. **`access-session-fixation-login`** (CWE-384, medium) — `app/routes/session.js:116`. Login writes `req.session.userId` onto the pre-existing session with no `req.session.regenerate()`. The exact fix is already applied 118 lines later for signup (`session.js:234`) and explained in a comment directly above the vulnerable line, but never applied to login.
45: 2. **`access-idor-allocations-userid`** (CWE-639, high) — `app/routes/allocations.js:16-18`. `displayAllocations` trusts `req.params.userId` with only `isLoggedIn` in front of it (`index.js:63`); the DAO query has no ownership filter. The commented-out fix (read the id from `req.session` instead) sits right above the vulnerable lines.
46: 3. **`access-benefits-get-missing-admin-check`** (CWE-862, medium) — `app/routes/index.js:55`. `isAdmin` middleware exists and is referenced two lines away in a comment, but not applied; any logged-in employee can list every non-admin employee's id, name and benefit date.
47: 4. **`access-benefits-post-missing-admin-check`** (CWE-862, high) — `app/routes/index.js:56`. Same missing `isAdmin`, but on the write path: `userId` comes from `req.body` with no relation to the caller's own session id, so any employee can overwrite any other employee's `benefitStartDate`.
48: 5. **`access-password-compare-plaintext-noncontanttime`** (CWE-916, medium) — `app/data/user-dao.js:61`. Passwords are stored verbatim (`user-dao.js:25`) and compared with `===`, both non-constant-time and plaintext; `bcrypt` is already imported and the constant-time replacement is commented out immediately below.
49: 6. **`access-login-no-rate-limit`** (CWE-307, medium) — `app/routes/index.js:34`. No counter, delay or lockout anywhere on the login path, and no rate-limiting dependency in `package.json`.
50: 7. **`access-csrf-profile-post`** (CWE-352, high) — `app/routes/index.js:48`. `csurf` is a declared dependency and `server.js` shows exactly where it would be wired in (`server.js:107`), but the `app.use(csrf())` line is commented out, so **no route in the app has CSRF protection** — this is the specific case of "CSRF middleware present in the dependency tree but never mounted." `/profile` is cited because it is the highest-impact state-changing route (bank account/routing, SSN, DOB); the same absent control applies to every other `POST`/`PUT` route in the table above.
51: 8. **`access-session-no-expiration`** (CWE-613, medium) — `server.js:78-85`. The `session()` call sets no `cookie` option at all, so the default `maxAge: null` applies and no session is ever marked expired by time; a drafted `cookie: { httpOnly: true }` block with a `TODO: Add maxAge` comment was never completed or enabled.
52: 
53: ## What was not covered
54: 
55: - **JWT**: this app uses `express-session` cookies exclusively; there is no JWT issuance or verification anywhere in `app/` or `config/`, so the JWT-pitfalls checks in the access skill do not apply and were not filed.
56: - **MFA**: the app has no MFA or "remember this device" mechanism at all; there is nothing to check here beyond noting its total absence, which is a design gap rather than a line-level finding.
57: - **`/memos` and `/contributions` CSRF**: the same missing global CSRF control found on `/profile` (finding 7) also applies to `POST /memos` (`index.js:67`) and `POST /contributions` (`index.js:52`); these are not filed as separate findings to avoid three near-identical entries for one root cause (the commented-out `csrf()` at `server.js:107`), but a fix there resolves all three.
58: - **Open redirect (`/learn`) and SSRF (`/research`)**: read and confirmed, but scoped to the injection/platform departments' CWE ids (CWE-601, CWE-918), not access/authorization, so left for them to file.
59: - **Cookie-secret hard-coding** (`config/env/all.js`, `development.js`, `test.js`, flagged by the local semgrep rule): this is a secrets-management issue (CWE-798), left for the secrets department.
60: - **`app/data/*-dao.js` files not reached from any route in this review** (`memos-dao.js`, `contributions-dao.js`, `research-dao.js`): read only far enough to confirm they take `userId` from `req.session` (via their handlers) rather than from the request directly; not traced further since no access-control gap was found on those paths.
61: - **Runtime behavior**: this is a static read only. Whether any reverse proxy, WAF, or infrastructure-level rate limiter sits in front of this app in a real deployment was not checked and cannot be from the source alone.
62: - **Dependency-level vulnerabilities** (e.g. inside `express-session`, `bcrypt-nodejs`, `consolidate`/`swig` themselves) are out of scope for this department; see the dependencies department's report.

(End of file - total 62 lines)
</content>

1: # Dependencies — NodeGoat
2: 
3: ## Scope and method
4: 
5: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (111 files locked in `target.json`, read-only for this review; nothing was written into it). This department covers CWE-1104 (unmaintained third-party components) and CWE-1357 (reliance on insufficiently trustworthy components), scored against the OWASP category A06:2021 – Vulnerable and Outdated Components.
6: 
7: 1. **Manifest.** Read `package.json` in full (65 lines). It declares 16 production dependencies (`dependencies`) and 20 development dependencies (`devDependencies`), every one as a semver range except four exact pins: `bcrypt-nodejs` (`0.0.3`), `marked` (`0.3.5`), `needle` (`2.2.4`) and `node-esapi` (`0.0.1`).
8: 2. **Lockfile.** `package-lock.json` is present (888 KB, `lockfileVersion` present), so it was used as the source of truth for *installed* versions, not the manifest ranges — a `^` range can silently resolve to any later compatible version at the next `npm install`, and several ranges here had already drifted (e.g. `mongodb` `^2.1.18` → installed `2.2.36`).
9: 3. **`npm audit --json`.** Run inside the target tree (`cd /root/targets/NodeGoat && npm audit --json`), which only reads `package.json`/`package-lock.json` and queries the npm registry's advisory database — it does not write into the tree. **The registry was reachable**: the JSON output carried no `error` field, returned a full `metadata.vulnerabilities` breakdown and a `vulnerabilities` object keyed by package name with GHSA ids, CVSS vectors, CWE ids and affected ranges for each. This is a live-registry result, not a fallback.
10: 4. **Registry cross-checks.** For packages the audit did not flag (`bcrypt-nodejs`, `node-esapi`) and for current-latest comparisons (`helmet`, `express`, `mongodb`, `marked`, `underscore`), `npm view <pkg> time deprecated version --json` was run against the same reachable registry to get publish dates, deprecation notices and current latest versions.
11: 5. **Semgrep.** `semgrep --version` printed `1.177.0`, so it is present. This department's remit is manifest/lockfile analysis, not source-level pattern matching, so semgrep was not run here; the code-level findings (injection, XSS, secrets, etc.) that a semgrep pass over this same tree would surface belong to the other departments (`injection`, `access`, `data`, `platform`) and are out of scope for this report.
12: 
13: ### Headline numbers
14: 
15: `npm audit --json`'s `metadata.vulnerabilities` for the full resolved graph (1,479 packages: 396 prod, 1,016 dev, 116 optional):
16: 
17: | info | low | moderate | high | critical | total |
18: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
19: | 0 | 8 | 33 | 66 | 38 | **145** |
20: 
21: Per this department's instruction not to report one finding per transitive package, `findings/dependencies.json` does **not** enumerate all 145 audit entries. 25: 10 findings in `findings/dependencies.json`: 4 critical, 4 high, 1 low, 1 info. 28: 
29: - **`dep-mongodb`** (`package.json:18`, `"mongodb": "^2.1.18"`) — resolves to `mongodb@2.2.36`. Own advisory GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r (DoS) plus 2 transitive advisory-carrying packages (`mongodb-core`, `bson`), the latter with a CVSS 9.8 deserialization advisory (GHSA-v8w9-2789-6hhr, CWE-502).

44: - **`dep-node-esapi`** (`package.json:20`, info) — no npm-audit advisory, no deprecation notice, but only ever published once (2014-01-31) and never updated since. Flagged info: a real gap, but with no evidence of active exploitation or known weakness.
45:

1: # Injection and traversal — NodeGoat
2: 
3: ## Scope and method
4: 
5: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (111 files locked in `target.json`, read-only for this review; nothing was written into the target tree). This is a language-model review grounded by a static scanner and by the mechanical examiner (`verify-safety-report.mjs`).
6: 
7: `semgrep 1.177.0` was available and was run from the target root with both the local pack (`/home/user/deepseek-harness/examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/program-code-safety/semgrep`) and the registry pack `p/owasp-top-ten` (the registry was reachable, so both packs ran together, `--metrics off`). It reported 29 raw hits across 113 rules over 72 git-tracked files. Every hit was treated as a place to read, not as a finding: several (GitHub Actions mutable tags, cookie-setting defaults, plaintext HTTP links in tutorial prose) belong to other departments (platform/dependencies) and are out of scope here; the injection-relevant hits (`$where` in `allocations-dao.js`, `eval` and string concatenation in `contributions.js`, the open redirect in `index.js`) were each read in full, in the surrounding handler and DAO, before being written up.
8: 
9: Following the review-method discipline, every route registered in `app/routes/index.js` and `app/routes/tutorial.js` was read first, then each handler was traced forward into its DAO and its template. Read in full: `server.js` (template-engine and session setup), `app/routes/*.js` (all eight route modules), `app/data/*.js` (all seven DAOs), and the views whose controllers pass request-derived data into them (`memos.html`, `profile.html`, `allocations.html`, `research.html`). `config/config.js` and `config/env/*.js` were read to confirm which values are environment-derived versus literal.
10: 
11: ## Findings
12: 
13: Ten findings, all `confirmed` — the tainted source, every intermediate function, and the sink were read for each, with no sanitizer or framework guard in between.
14: 
15: ### Critical
16: 
17: - **`injection-eval-pretax`**, **`injection-eval-aftertax`**, **`injection-eval-roth`** — `app/routes/contributions.js:32-34`. `POST /contributions` passes `req.body.preTax`, `req.body.afterTax` and `req.body.roth` straight into `eval()`, three separate calls, three separate sinks. Validation (`isNaN`/negative checks) runs only after `eval` has already executed. Any authenticated user can run arbitrary JavaScript in the server process — full remote code execution, not merely a query- or markup-level injection. Fix: replace each `eval(...)` with `Number(...)`/`parseInt(...)` plus a `NaN` check, exactly as the disabled fix already commented into the same file demonstrates.
18: 
19: ### High
20: 
21: - **`injection-nosql-where-allocations`** — `app/data/allocations-dao.js:78`. `threshold` flows unvalidated from `GET /allocations/:userId?threshold=...` (`app/routes/allocations.js:20`) into a MongoDB `$where` clause built by template-literal interpolation, letting an attacker run arbitrary JavaScript inside the MongoDB server (denial of service, or reading other users' allocation data by injecting an always-true expression). Fix: bound-check `threshold` as an integer and use a plain query object (`{ userId, stocks: { $gt: threshold } }`), never a `$where` string, matching the disabled fix already present in the file.
22: - **`injection-ssrf-research`** — `app/routes/research.js:16`. `GET /research` concatenates `req.query.url` and `req.query.symbol` — both fully attacker-controlled query parameters, the form's hidden `url` field only pre-fills the browser UI and is not enforced server-side — into a URL handed to `needle.get()`, and the fetched body is written back to the client raw. An attacker can point this at an internal address or a cloud metadata endpoint and read the response through the app. Fix: allowlist the destination host, block private/link-local/metadata ranges, and re-check the resolved IP before the request.
23: - **`injection-redos-profile-bankrouting`** — `app/routes/profile.js:61`. `POST /profile` runs the nested-quantifier pattern `/([0-9]+)+\#/` (line 59, the file's own comment names it as the vulnerable form, with the one-character fix commented out directly above it) against `req.body.bankRouting` with no length cap. A crafted value with many digits and no trailing `#` triggers catastrophic backtracking and pins the single-threaded Node event loop, denying service to every user of the process, not just the attacker. Fix: drop the outer `+` (`/([0-9]+)\#/`, as already shown in the disabled fix) and cap the input length before testing.
24: - **`injection-xss-memos-marked`** — `app/views/memos.html:31`. `req.body.memo` is stored unsanitized (`app/data/memos-dao.js`) and rendered through `{{ marked(doc.memo) }}` with swig's `autoescape` globally disabled (`server.js:137`); the only remaining guard is `marked`'s own deprecated, bypassable `sanitize: true` option. Any logged-in user can plant markup that executes in every other viewer's browser when they open `/memos`. Fix: re-enable swig autoescaping and sanitize the rendered HTML with an allowlist library (e.g. DOMPurify) immediately before the raw-output sink.
25: 
26: ### Medium
27: 
28: - **`injection-open-redirect-learn`** — `app/routes/index.js:72`. `GET /learn` redirects to `req.query.url` with no allowlist or relative-path check — a classic open-redirect usable for phishing from a trusted NodeGoat link. Fix: allowlist destination hosts/paths or restrict to relative, in-application paths.
29: - **`injection-xss-profile-firstname-value`** and **`injection-xss-profile-firstname-href`** — `app/views/profile.html:41` and `:78`. When the profile-update form's bank-routing regex rejects a submission, `app/routes/profile.js:64` echoes `req.body.firstName` back unencoded as `firstNameSafeString`, which two separate template sinks place — once inside an `value` attribute, once inside an `href` attribute (as a `javascript:` URI) — with swig autoescaping disabled. Each is a distinct sink an attacker can trigger independently (attribute breakout vs. `javascript:` scheme). Fix: re-enable autoescaping, and for the `href` context specifically, URL-encode into a separate field as the code's own `@FIXME` comment already prescribes.
30: 
31: ## What was not covered
32: 
33: - **Client-side JavaScript and the bundled vendor libraries** (`app/assets/vendor/*`, `app/assets/js/*`) were not reviewed for DOM-based sinks (`innerHTML`, `document.write`); these are third-party or non-request-driven assets and were out of scope for this pass.
34: - **`app/assets/js/tour/redirects-steps.js`** and the tutorial content pages (`app/views/tutorial/*.html`) were skimmed for structure but not traced line-by-line; they are static walkthrough pages, not live request handlers, except where `tutorial.js` renders them by a fixed, hardcoded page list (`app/routes/tutorial.js:15-28`), which is not attacker-influenced and was not written up.
35: - **CSRF, session-cookie flags, and authentication/authorization logic** (e.g. `app/routes/session.js`'s login/signup flow, the missing `isAdmin` check on `/benefits`) are access-control and session-management concerns, not injection, and are left to the `access` department; they were read only far enough to confirm they don't also constitute an injection sink.
36: - **Dependency-level vulnerabilities** (e.g. the pinned `marked@0.3.5`, whose `sanitize` option is deprecated in later releases and was never a complete HTML sanitizer) are named here only as forming part of the `memos.html` finding's evidence; a full advisory lookup against `package.json`/`package-lock.json` is the `dependencies` department's job and was not performed.
37: - **Runtime/deployment configuration** — actual environment variables, reverse-proxy or WAF rules, and whether `NODE_ENV=production` changes any of the behaviors above — was not available to a static read and is not confirmed either way.
38: - No SQL findings are reported because NodeGoat has no relational-database layer; all persistence is through the MongoDB driver, covered under the NoSQL/`$where` finding above.

(End of file - total 38 lines)
</content>

8: 
9: Beyond the semgrep hits, this department manually read: every file under `config/`; `server.js`; `app/data/*.js` (all six DAOs); `app/routes/session.js`; `artifacts/db-reset.js`; `artifacts/cert/server.key` and `server.crt`; `docker-compose.yml`; `Dockerfile`; `app.json`; `Procfile`; `.travis.yml`; `package.json`; `README.md`; `test/security/profile-test.js`; the three `test/e2e/fixtures/users/*.json` files; and the tutorial pages that reference credentials (`app/views/tutorial/a1.html`, `a6.html`, `a7.html`). No `.env`, `.npmrc`, or `.netrc` file exists in the tree (confirmed with a targeted filename search); the connection-string placeholders in `README.md` (`mongodb://<username>:<password>@...`) are template syntax with angle-bracket placeholders, not filled-in values, and are not reported as findings.
10: 
11: Every finding below quotes a line this department actually read, with a file, a line number, and a snippet that matches the target's text verbatim (confirmed by `node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/secrets.json`, which reports 5/5 verified).
12: 
13: ## Findings
14: 
15: ### Critical
16: 
17: - **`secrets-default-admin-password`** — `artifacts/db-reset.js:18`, CWE-798, confidence `confirmed`. 19: ### High

22: 
23: ### Medium
24: 
25: - **`secrets-committed-rsa-private-key`** — `artifacts/cert/server.key:1-15`, CWE-321, confidence `confirmed`. A full PEM RSA private key is committed to the repository. 26: 
27: ### Low
28: 
29: - **`secrets-zap-api-key-default-config`** — `config/env/development.js:6`, CWE-798, confidence `confirmed`.
